name: Omoplata from Crackhead Control
description: Master the omoplata from Crackhead Control. Complete guide to this 10th Planet shoulder lock entry with finishing mechanics, defensive counters, and drills.
target_area: Shoulder joint (rotator cuff, capsule, AC joint)
overview:
The omoplata from Crackhead Control leverages the unique arm and posture control inherent in the 10th Planet Rubber Guard system to create a high-percentage shoulder lock entry. From Crackhead Control, the bottom player already controls the opponent's posture and near arm through the characteristic overhook and leg positioning, creating an ideal platform for threading the attacking leg across the shoulder into the omoplata. The pre-existing arm isolation eliminates the most difficult prerequisite for successful omoplata attacks from other guard positions.

What distinguishes this entry from standard closed guard omoplata attempts is the pre-broken posture and trapped arm. In Crackhead Control, the opponent's arm is already isolated between the attacker's legs and their posture is fully compromised, allowing the guard player to focus entirely on the leg thread and hip escape rather than simultaneously managing posture breaks and arm control. This makes the setup faster and significantly more reliable than omoplata entries from basic guard.

The finishing mechanics follow established omoplata principles once the perpendicular angle is achieved. The attacker controls the opponent's far hip to prevent the forward roll escape, sits up tall to maximize the lever arm, and applies progressive forward pressure to externally rotate the shoulder joint past its natural range of motion. Competition data from no-gi events shows this entry yields notably higher finish rates than omoplata attempts from basic closed guard, primarily because the opponent's defensive options are severely limited by the preceding Rubber Guard control sequence.

injury_risks.recovery_time: 6-12 weeks for minor tears, 3-6 months for major tears

safety_considerations.application_speed: SLOW and progressive - 4-6 seconds minimum pressure increase
tap_signals: Physical hand tap on opponent or mat
Physical foot tap on opponent or mat
release_protocol: Immediately stop all forward pressure and rotation
Allow opponent to extract arm slowly
training_restrictions: Never spike or jerk the shoulder rotation
Never apply competition speed in training
Always allow opponent access to tap
Stop immediately if opponent rolls forward (escape attempt)
Never apply full finishing pressure until advanced belt level
Always control the rate of shoulder rotation

variations_and_setups.when_to_use: When you have a secure Crackhead Control with fully broken posture and the overhook is tight on the near arm

attacker.name: from Crackhead Control Attacker
attacker.description: Learn to attack with the omoplata from Crackhead Control. Step-by-step setup, execution, and counter responses for this Rubber Guard shoulder lock technique.
attacker.overview: Attacking with the omoplata from Crackhead Control provides a systematic path from Rubber Guard control to a high-percentage shoulder lock finish. The pre-existing arm isolation and broken posture from Crackhead Control eliminate the setup phase that makes standard omoplata entries unreliable. The guard player can focus entirely on smooth leg threading, decisive hip escaping to create the perpendicular finishing angle, and disciplined hip control to prevent the forward roll escape that accounts for the majority of failed omoplata attempts across all entry positions.
key_principles: Break posture completely in Crackhead Control before initiating the leg thread to prevent the opponent from posturing out during the transition
Thread the attacking leg smoothly across the opponent's shoulder line without releasing the overhook or creating space for posture recovery
Hip escape decisively to create the perpendicular angle that generates shoulder rotation leverage against the trapped arm
Establish two-handed control on the opponent's far hip before attempting to finish to eliminate the forward roll escape
Sit up tall and walk hands forward to maximize the lever arm on the shoulder joint during the finishing sequence
Maintain constant downward pressure on the opponent's back with your legs to prevent them from sitting up or stacking
setup_requirements: Established Crackhead Control with opponent's posture completely broken and head driven toward the mat
Overhook secured on opponent's near arm with their elbow trapped past your hip line between your legs
Attacking leg positioned to swing freely across opponent's shoulder and upper back without obstruction
Opponent's base compromised through sustained posture breaking so they cannot explosively posture during the transition

execution_steps.description: Verify the overhook is tight on the opponent's near arm and their posture is fully broken with their forehead near the mat. Your shin should be positioned across the back of their neck with your foot grabbed. This foundation determines whether the omoplata entry will succeed.

Release the shin from behind the opponent's neck and swing your attacking leg over their trapped arm, threading it across their shoulder and upper back. Maintain the overhook grip throughout this transition to prevent the arm from slipping free as the leg crosses over.

Execute a strong hip escape away from the opponent, pivoting your body to create a perpendicular angle to their torso. Your hips must clear past their shoulder line so that your thigh rests firmly across the back of their shoulder with their arm pinned between your legs.

Immediately grip the opponent's far hip or belt line with both hands to prevent the forward roll escape. Your inside leg should hook across their lower back while your outside leg posts on the mat for base. This is the single most critical step for finishing success.

Walk your hands forward on the mat while sitting your torso upright and perpendicular to the opponent. Their arm should be trapped between your legs with their elbow pointed toward the ceiling and the shoulder already under significant rotational tension from the angle.

Lean forward progressively, driving your chest toward the mat in front of you while keeping the opponent's arm pinned against your hip. Apply slow, steady pressure that externally rotates their shoulder joint. Increase force gradually over 4-6 seconds until the opponent taps.

common_counters.counter: Forward roll escape to relieve shoulder pressure before hip control is established
common_counters.your_response: Follow their roll by maintaining leg control on the arm and immediately transition to mount or re-establish the omoplata from the new angle by staying connected to the trapped arm throughout the rotation

common_counters.counter: Posturing up explosively before the leg thread completes across the shoulder
common_counters.your_response: Immediately switch to triangle choke setup using the partially threaded leg to close around their neck, or return to Mission Control by resetting the shin across the back of their neck to re-establish Rubber Guard control

common_counters.counter: Stacking body weight forward to collapse the perpendicular finishing angle
common_counters.your_response: Frame against their hip with your free hand and use your leg hooks to redirect their pressure laterally. Angle your hips further away to maintain the perpendicular position and continue the finishing sequence with increased urgency

common_errors.error: Rushing the leg thread before posture is fully broken in Crackhead Control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent postures up during the transition and extracts their arm, losing the entire omoplata setup and potentially the guard position
common_errors.correction: Confirm posture is completely broken with forehead near the mat before initiating any leg movement from Crackhead Control

common_errors.error: Failing to hip escape far enough to create the perpendicular finishing angle
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient leverage on the shoulder joint, allowing the opponent to stack forward and recover posture or pass the guard
common_errors.correction: Hip escape until your hip clears past their shoulder line and your body forms a clear right angle to their torso

common_errors.error: Not controlling the opponent's far hip before attempting to finish
common_errors.consequence: Opponent performs the forward roll escape, the highest-percentage omoplata defense, potentially reversing to top position
common_errors.correction: Always establish two-handed hip control before sitting up to finish - prioritize this over speed of the finishing sequence

common_errors.error: Leaning backward instead of driving chest forward during the finishing pressure
common_errors.consequence: Removes the mechanical advantage from the shoulder lock and allows opponent to sit up, extract their arm, and escape
common_errors.correction: Walk hands forward and drive chest toward the mat in front of you while keeping the trapped arm pinned against your hip

common_errors.error: Releasing the overhook too early during the leg thread transition
common_errors.consequence: Opponent's arm slips free before the leg is fully threaded across the shoulder, nullifying the entire attack sequence
common_errors.correction: Maintain the overhook grip until your leg is fully threaded and positioned across the shoulder, only releasing to transition to hip control

common_errors.error: Allowing space between your thigh and the opponent's shoulder during the finish
common_errors.consequence: Opponent extracts their arm through the gap between your thigh and their shoulder, escaping the submission entirely
common_errors.correction: Keep your thigh tight against the back of their shoulder by squeezing your legs together and maintaining constant downward pressure

knowledge_assessment.question: What anatomical structures does the omoplata from Crackhead Control primarily attack?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The omoplata attacks the shoulder joint through forced external rotation, primarily targeting the rotator cuff muscles (supraspinatus, infraspinatus, teres minor, subscapularis), the glenohumeral capsule, and the AC joint. The lever created by your legs against the trapped arm generates rotational force that exceeds the shoulder's natural range of motion, creating a submission through joint hyperextension and capsular stress.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent starts to posture up as you begin threading your leg across their shoulder - what adjustment prevents escape?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Immediately abandon the omoplata entry and switch to a triangle choke by closing your legs around their neck and arm, or return to Mission Control by resetting the shin across the back of their neck. Forcing the omoplata against a posturing opponent burns energy and creates scramble situations that favor the top player. The partially threaded leg provides a platform for alternative attacks rather than requiring a full position reset.

knowledge_assessment.question: What control must be established before attempting the finishing pressure, and why is it the most critical step?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Two-handed control on the opponent's far hip or belt line must be established before sitting up to finish. This eliminates the forward roll escape, which is the highest-percentage defense against all omoplata variations. Without hip control, even a mechanically perfect finishing angle will fail because the opponent can simply somersault forward to relieve shoulder pressure. Securing the hip before finishing is more important than speed or angle precision.

knowledge_assessment.question: At what point during the omoplata sequence is the opponent past the point of safe escape without risking injury?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The point of no safe escape occurs when the attacker has achieved the perpendicular angle with hip control established and begins sitting up with forward pressure. At this stage, the shoulder is already under significant rotational stress and explosive escape attempts risk acute injury to the rotator cuff or labrum. The shoulder's available range of motion is fully consumed, and any sudden force from either direction can cause immediate damage requiring surgical intervention.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the three most common finishing errors and what underlying cause do they share?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The three most common errors are leaning backward instead of driving the chest forward toward the mat, failing to control the far hip which allows the forward roll escape, and creating space between your thigh and the opponent's shoulder which permits arm extraction. All three share a common root cause of insufficient body positioning discipline during the finishing sequence, typically caused by rushing to finish rather than methodically establishing each control point.

knowledge_assessment.question: How should your grip placement change during the transition from Crackhead Control through to the omoplata finish?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Begin with the overhook grip on the opponent's near arm during Crackhead Control. Maintain this grip throughout the leg thread until your leg is fully across their shoulder. Then release the overhook and transition both hands to the opponent's far hip to prevent the roll escape. As you sit up to finish, one hand remains controlling the hip while the other walks forward on the mat for additional forward driving pressure. Never release the overhook before the leg thread is complete.

knowledge_assessment.question: What are the immediate safety protocols when the opponent signals a tap during the omoplata finish?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Upon receiving any tap signal, immediately stop all forward pressure and cease shoulder rotation. Release the leg pinch on the shoulder by opening your legs and allowing the arm to move freely. Do not maintain the position while checking on your partner. The shoulder joint can sustain acute damage from even momentary additional pressure after the tap, particularly rotator cuff tears and labrum injuries that may require surgical repair and months of rehabilitation.

knowledge_assessment.question: How does the Crackhead Control entry change competition finishing strategy compared to a standard closed guard omoplata?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The Crackhead Control entry provides pre-broken posture and arm isolation that standard entries lack, allowing more aggressive commitment to the finish once the leg thread completes. In competition, this means faster transitions from setup to finish with fewer defensive windows for the opponent. The reduced setup time forces opponents to face the finishing sequence before their defensive reactions fully engage, yielding higher tap rates compared to entries requiring simultaneous posture breaking and arm isolation.

knowledge_assessment.question: Your opponent grabs your ankle to block the leg thread - how do you respond?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Use your free hand to strip their grip on your ankle while maintaining the overhook on their arm. If the grip cannot be broken immediately, redirect to a triangle choke by using the blocked leg to close around their neck from the current angle. Alternatively, pummel the foot free by circling it behind their elbow and threading from the opposite direction. Never force the leg thread against a secured grip as this wastes energy and telegraphs the attack pattern.

knowledge_assessment.question: What breathing pattern maximizes finishing pressure while maintaining training safety?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Exhale steadily as you apply forward pressure during the finish, using each breath cycle to incrementally increase the rotational force on the shoulder. Avoid holding your breath, which creates muscular tension and reduces your ability to feel the opponent's resistance for controlled application. Rhythmic breathing prevents applying the submission too explosively, which is critical for training safety and gives the opponent adequate time to recognize and signal a tap before injury occurs.

defender.name: from Crackhead Control Defender
defender.description: Defend against the omoplata from Crackhead Control. Recognition cues, escape techniques, and survival strategies against this Rubber Guard shoulder lock.
defender.overview: Defending the omoplata from Crackhead Control requires early recognition and prevention rather than late-stage escape attempts. The Rubber Guard system's pre-existing posture control means the omoplata setup begins from an already disadvantaged position, making the initial leg thread the critical defensive window. Once the perpendicular angle is established with hip control, escape options narrow dramatically and injury risk increases with each second of delay. Successful defense depends on recognizing the transition from Crackhead Control retention to omoplata attack and responding within the narrow window before the leg threads across the shoulder.
key_principles: Maintain posture aggressively to prevent Crackhead Control from fully establishing before the omoplata is initiated
Recognize the leg thread initiation as the primary defensive trigger and react immediately by posturing or extracting the arm
Keep elbows tight to your body to prevent the attacking leg from crossing over your shoulder line
If caught in the omoplata, address hip control first before attempting to posture up or roll forward
Execute the forward roll escape only before the opponent establishes hip control - not after
Tap early if the perpendicular angle is achieved with hip control secured, as late escapes from deep omoplata risk serious shoulder injury
recognition_cues: Opponent releases their shin from behind your neck while tightening or maintaining the overhook grip on your arm, signaling the transition from Crackhead Control to omoplata attack
You feel your arm being progressively isolated between the opponent's legs with increasing downward pressure across the back of your shoulder and upper arm
Opponent's hips begin scooting away from you laterally while their leg swings up and over your shoulder and upper back in an arcing motion
The overhook grip shifts from controlling your posture to actively pinning your arm against the opponent's hip as their body angle changes

defensive_options.action: Posture up explosively before the leg thread completes
defensive_options.when_to_use: When you feel the opponent releasing the shin from behind your neck and beginning the leg swing - this is the earliest and best defensive window
defensive_options.if_successful: Opponent loses arm isolation and must reset to Crackhead Control or another Rubber Guard position
defensive_options.risk: If timed late, opponent may switch to triangle choke using the partially threaded leg

defensive_options.action: Forward roll escape before hip control is established
defensive_options.when_to_use: After the leg has threaded across your shoulder but before the opponent grips your far hip with both hands
defensive_options.if_successful: Completely relieves shoulder pressure and may result in achieving top position after the roll
defensive_options.risk: If opponent follows the roll maintaining arm control, you may end up in mount with the arm still trapped

defensive_options.action: Stack and drive body weight forward to collapse the finishing angle
defensive_options.when_to_use: When the opponent has threaded the leg but has not yet completed the hip escape to the full perpendicular angle
defensive_options.if_successful: Crushes the omoplata angle and forces opponent to abandon the attack or transition to basic guard
defensive_options.risk: If the perpendicular angle is already established, stacking increases rotational pressure on your own shoulder

escape_paths: Forward roll when hip control is not yet established, somersaulting over the trapped arm to completely relieve shoulder pressure and potentially achieve top position
Stack and drive body weight forward to collapse the opponent's angle before they achieve the perpendicular finishing position
Strip the overhook grip during the leg thread transition and extract the trapped arm before the omoplata is fully established

favorable_outcomes.how: Posture up early before the leg thread completes, extracting your arm and forcing the opponent to reset their Rubber Guard position from scratch
Stack forward after a partial omoplata attempt collapses the finishing angle, forcing the opponent to abandon the attack and settle for basic closed guard

common_errors.error: Attempting the forward roll escape after the opponent has already secured two-handed hip control
common_errors.consequence: Opponent follows the roll maintaining arm control and transitions to mount or re-establishes the omoplata from a worse angle, with increased injury risk during the dynamic movement
common_errors.correction: Only attempt the forward roll before hip control is established - if you feel both hands gripping your far hip, the roll window has closed and you should tap rather than risk injury

common_errors.error: Reaching back with the free arm to push the opponent's legs away from your shoulder
common_errors.consequence: Exposes the free arm to additional attacks including triangle choke or arm lock variations, potentially creating a worse submission situation
common_errors.correction: Use the free arm to post on the mat for base or to strip the overhook grip during the transition phase, never reach backward toward the opponent's legs

common_errors.error: Delaying the tap when the omoplata is fully locked with the perpendicular angle and hip control established
common_errors.consequence: Risk of acute rotator cuff tear, labrum damage, or AC joint separation that may require surgical intervention and months of rehabilitation
common_errors.correction: Tap immediately once you feel shoulder pressure that you cannot relieve through technical movement - the margin between controlled pressure and injury is very small with shoulder locks

common_errors.error: Trying to muscle out of the omoplata using strength rather than technical escape
common_errors.consequence: Rapid fatigue while the opponent maintains positional leverage, and explosive escape attempts increase the risk of self-inflicted shoulder injury
common_errors.correction: Use technical escapes based on timing and positioning - posture recovery, forward roll, or stacking must be executed at the correct moment rather than forced through strength

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you recognize the omoplata from Crackhead Control is being set up?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The primary recognition cue is the opponent releasing their shin from behind your neck while maintaining or tightening the overhook grip on your arm. This signals the transition from Crackhead Control retention to omoplata attack. You will also feel the attacking leg beginning to swing over your shoulder and increased downward pressure isolating your arm between the opponent's legs as they reposition for the submission.

knowledge_assessment.question: What is the safest way to signal a tap to the omoplata from Crackhead Control?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Tap immediately and clearly using your free hand on the opponent's body or the mat, giving multiple rapid taps to ensure the signal is recognized. Simultaneously vocalize a verbal tap for redundancy. Tap as soon as you feel shoulder pressure that exceeds your ability to escape through technique. Do not wait for pain - the transition from controlled pressure to structural injury is rapid with shoulder locks, and rotator cuff damage can require months of rehabilitation.

knowledge_assessment.question: What defensive options are available against the omoplata from Crackhead Control and when should each be used?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The three primary defenses in priority order are posturing up early before the leg thread completes, executing a forward roll before hip control is established, and stacking forward to collapse the finishing angle. Each defense has a specific timing window and attempting them outside that window either fails or worsens your position. Recognition speed and reaction timing matter more than strength for all three options.

knowledge_assessment.question: When does the forward roll escape become too dangerous to attempt?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The forward roll becomes extremely risky once the opponent has established two-handed control on your far hip and has achieved the perpendicular angle with their torso. At this point, they can follow your roll while maintaining arm control, potentially ending in mount with the arm still trapped. Attempting a late roll also puts the shoulder under dynamic loading during the rotation, significantly increasing acute injury risk compared to a controlled tap.
